a: Tokenization splits text into tokens — the subword chunks LLMs actually process (e.g. 'unbelievable' might become 'un' + 'believ' + 'able'). Each token maps to an ID in the model's vocabulary (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece are common algorithms). It matters practically: cost and context limits are counted in tokens (~4 characters in English), and tokenization quirks explain why models struggle with character-level tasks like counting letters.

Embeddings map items (words, sentences, images, users) into dense numeric vectors where geometric closeness means semantic similarity — 'king' and 'queen' end up near each other, and even relationships compose (king - man + woman ≈ queen). They are the foundation of semantic search, RAG, clustering, and recommendation: anything you can embed, you can retrieve by meaning instead of exact keywords.

Attention lets each token look at every other token and decide which ones matter for its own representation: it computes queries, keys, and values, takes dot products between a token's query and all keys to get attention scores (how relevant each token is), normalizes them with softmax into weights, and blends the values by those weights. 'Self'-attention means tokens attend within the same sequence. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel so different heads learn different relationships (syntax, coreference, position).

The transformer stacks blocks of (multi-head self-attention + feed-forward network), with residual connections and layer normalization around each, plus positional information because attention itself is order-blind. Variants: encoder-only (BERT — bidirectional understanding), decoder-only (GPT — causal, predicts the next token; the dominant LLM form), and encoder-decoder (T5, translation). The feed-forward layers hold much of the factual knowledge; attention routes information between tokens.

Attention is permutation-invariant — it has no sense of word order on its own, so position must be injected. Original transformers added fixed sinusoidal position vectors; modern models learn positional embeddings or use RoPE (rotary embeddings, used by LLaMA-family), which rotates queries/keys so attention scores depend on relative distance. This is what lets the model know 'dog bites man' differs from 'man bites dog'.

The KV cache stores each token's keys and values from previous attention layers so they are not recomputed for every new token during generation — without it, generating token 1000 would recompute attention over all 999 previous tokens from scratch. It makes autoregressive generation roughly O(1) per new token instead of O(n), at the cost of GPU memory that grows with context length (which is why long contexts are expensive and why techniques like multi-query attention exist).

Sampling parameters control randomness in generation. Temperature divides logits before softmax: low temperature (< 1) sharpens the distribution — focused, deterministic, repetitive; high temperature flattens it — creative but riskier. Top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens; top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set whose probabilities sum to p (e.g. 0.9), dynamically widening when the model is uncertain. Factual/extraction work: low temperature; brainstorming: higher.

LLM training has stages: (1) pretraining — next-token prediction on massive text corpora, learning language and world knowledge (the expensive part: trillions of tokens); (2) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) — training on high-quality instruction-response pairs to follow instructions; (3) preference alignment — RLHF or DPO, tuning on human preference comparisons so outputs become helpful, safe, and well-formatted. RLHF trains a reward model from human rankings and optimizes the policy against it; DPO skips the reward model and optimizes directly on preference pairs.

Hallucination is when a model states false information fluently and confidently. Causes: it is trained to produce plausible continuations, not verified facts; knowledge is frozen at training cutoff; and pressure to answer even when unsure. Mitigations: ground it with retrieval (RAG so it cites real sources), lower temperature, allow 'I don't know' in the system prompt, ask for citations, and keep a human in the loop for high-stakes outputs. It cannot be fully eliminated — design systems assuming it will happen.

Prompt engineering is designing inputs that reliably get the behavior you want: give context and a role ('You are a senior reviewer...'); show the task with one or few examples (few-shot); ask for step-by-step reasoning on hard problems (chain-of-thought); specify the output format explicitly (JSON schema, bullet list); and decompose complex jobs into chained prompts. Biggest practical wins: be specific about format and constraints, and provide examples of exactly what you want.

Zero-shot means asking without examples ('Classify this review as positive or negative'); few-shot means including a handful of demonstrations in the prompt, which steers format and style through in-context learning — no weight updates involved. Few-shot dramatically improves consistency on niche formats and domains. Cost trade-off: examples consume context tokens, so use 2-5 strong, diverse examples rather than many mediocre ones.

Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step before answering, which substantially improves math, logic, and multi-step tasks — the intermediate tokens give the model more compute on the problem. Variants: 'Let's think step by step' (zero-shot CoT), worked examples (few-shot CoT), and tree-of-thought (branching and evaluating multiple reasoning paths). Trade-off: more output tokens = more latency and cost; and reasoning traces can still be confidently wrong.

The context window is how many tokens the model can process in one go — prompt plus generated output together (from 4k in early models to 128k-1M+ now). Attention cost grows quadratically with length, which is why long context is expensive and why KV-cache memory becomes the bottleneck. A bigger window does not guarantee use of all of it — models often lose recall in the middle of very long contexts ('lost in the middle'), so put critical info at the start or end.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) grounds an LLM in your data: (1) chunk your documents, (2) embed chunks into vectors, (3) at query time embed the question and retrieve the most similar chunks, (4) stuff them into the prompt as context, and (5) the LLM answers citing that context. Why it beats fine-tuning for knowledge: it is updatable instantly (re-index), cheaper, auditable (answers point to sources), and reduces hallucination — the model reads the answer instead of recalling it.

Chunking splits documents into retrievable pieces — the most underestimated RAG design choice. Too small: chunks lack context ('it' referring to nothing); too large: retrieval gets blurry and dilutes the LLM's attention. Common practice: 300-800 tokens with 10-20% overlap, respecting natural boundaries (headings, paragraphs). Better: semantic or structure-aware chunking, and adding metadata (title, section, date) to each chunk so retrieval can filter.

A vector database stores embeddings and finds nearest neighbors fast using approximate nearest neighbor indexes (HNSW, IVF). Choices: managed (Pinecone, Weaviate), embedded (FAISS, Chroma), or an extension on your existing Postgres (pgvector) — often the pragmatic choice since it keeps vectors next to relational data. Key concepts: cosine vs dot-product similarity, index/recall trade-off, metadata filtering, and hybrid search (vectors + keywords).

Hybrid search combines dense vector retrieval (understands meaning: 'car insurance' matches 'auto coverage') with sparse keyword search like BM25 (exact matches on product codes, names, rare terms). Results are fused — commonly with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) — getting the best of both. It matters because pure vector search misses exact identifiers and rare terms, which is a real failure mode in production RAG.

Reranking is the second stage of retrieval: a fast first pass (vector search) pulls 50-100 candidates, then a cross-encoder reads query and candidate together and scores them precisely — much more accurate but too slow to run over everything. This two-stage design gets near-cross-encoder quality at vector-search speed and measurably improves answer quality in production RAG.

An AI agent is an LLM put in a loop with tools and a goal: it reasons about the task, decides which tool to call (search, code execution, APIs — via function calling), observes the result, and iterates until done. The core loop is reason → act → observe → repeat (ReAct pattern). What separates a demo from production: constrained tool design, validation of tool arguments, iteration limits, and evaluation of whole trajectories, not just final answers.

Multi-agent systems split work among specialized roles (planner, coder, critic, researcher) that collaborate — often catching errors a single model misses via debate and review. Frameworks: LangGraph (graph-structured state machines, best control), CrewAI (role-based crews), AutoGen (conversational agents). Honest trade-off: more agents = more cost, latency, and failure modes; start single-agent and split only when a role genuinely needs its own context or tools.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data sources — think USB-C for AI integrations: a server exposes tools, resources, and prompts through a uniform protocol, and any MCP-capable client can use them without custom glue code for each pairing. It solves the N x M integration problem (N apps x M tools) that plagued function calling.

The decision ladder: prompt engineering first (cheapest, instant); RAG when the model lacks knowledge that changes often or must be cited; fine-tuning when you need to change behavior, style, or format — teaching the model HOW to respond — or to distill a smaller cheaper model. Not fine-tuning for facts that expire (you would retrain for every update). They combine well: fine-tune for format/tone, RAG for fresh knowledge.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tunes by freezing the base model weights and training tiny low-rank matrices injected into attention layers — often <1% of parameters. Benefits: a fraction of the GPU memory, adapters are small (MBs, swap-able per task on one base model), and no catastrophic forgetting of the base skills. QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization of the frozen base so a 70B model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU.

Quantization stores model weights in fewer bits (FP16 → INT8 → INT4), shrinking memory 2-4x and speeding inference with minor quality loss (larger drops below 4-bit). Post-training quantization (GPTQ, AWQ) works on a finished model; quantization-aware training bakes it in. It is what makes local inference of big models possible on consumer hardware — and QLoRA possible.

Knowledge distillation trains a small 'student' model to mimic a large 'teacher' — often on the teacher's soft probability outputs, which carry richer signal than hard labels. The student approaches teacher quality at a fraction of the serving cost/latency. It is the standard route to production efficiency: distill the expensive model into a cheap one, then verify the quality gap is acceptable for your task.

LLM evaluation layers: automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE for overlap — weak proxies), benchmark suites (MMLU, HumanEval — useful but contaminated over time), LLM-as-judge (a strong model scores outputs against a rubric — scalable but watch position/style bias), and human evaluation (gold standard, expensive). Production practice: build task-specific eval sets from real failures, run them in CI on every prompt or model change, and track them like unit tests — 'evals are the new unit tests'.

Guardrails wrap an LLM with checks on both sides: input — jailbreak/prompt-injection detection (user text like 'ignore previous instructions' or hidden instructions in retrieved documents), PII redaction, topic filters; output — schema validation (JSON parse + repair), toxicity/toxicity classifiers, and human escalation paths. Prompt injection is the signature LLM security threat: never give an agent authoritative powers (payments, deletes) without separate authorization layers — treat model output as untrusted input.

LLM cost management: route tasks by size (cheap model for classification, big model only for hard reasoning); cache (exact-match caches for repeated prompts, semantic caches for near-duplicates); shorten prompts (prompt compression, trim few-shots); batch offline work; cap max output tokens; and consider self-hosting small quantized models for high-volume simple tasks. Measure cost per resolved task, not per token — a pricier model that succeeds first try can be cheaper overall.

Inference latency is usually discussed as time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token speed. Controls: streaming (start showing tokens immediately — perceived latency drops even when total time does not), smaller or quantized models, KV-cache reuse across requests (prefix caching), speculative decoding (a small model drafts, the big one verifies), and batching trade-offs (higher throughput = higher per-request latency). Set an SLO on TTFT for chat UX; it dominates perceived quality.

vLLM is the standard open-source serving engine for self-hosted LLMs: PagedAttention manages KV-cache memory like virtual memory pages (eliminating fragmentation), enabling continuous batching that packs requests in and out dynamically — throughput often many times naive serving. Alternatives: TGI (Hugging Face), TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, max performance), SGLang. Knowing why batching + memory management dominate throughput is the interview-level insight.

LLMOps extends MLOps for LLM specifics: version prompts like code (prompt registry, changes reviewed via evals); trace every call (inputs, outputs, latency, cost — LangSmith/LangFuse); monitor quality in production (sample and judge outputs, track drift in failure rates); manage costs per feature; and A/B test model or prompt upgrades behind evals and canaries. The failure modes are new (hallucination, injection, format drift) but the discipline is classic: measure, version, roll back.

Multimodal models process multiple modalities in one system — text + images (GPT-4V, Gemini), audio (speech-to-text, voice assistants), video. Architecturally usually a modality encoder (e.g. vision transformer) projected into the LLM's token space, so the LLM reasons over image 'tokens'. Practical interview points: evaluation differs per modality, image tokens consume context fast, and real systems often bolt specialized models (OCR, ASR) around the LLM rather than one model doing everything.

Choosing a model: define the task and constraints first (accuracy bar, latency, privacy, budget). Build a small eval set of your real cases, test 3-4 candidates (frontier API models, mid-tier, open-source like Llama/Mistral/Qwen), and pick the cheapest that passes. Consider: closed APIs = fastest to quality, per-token cost, data leaves your perimeter; open weights = control, fine-tuning freedom, infra burden. Revisit quarterly — the frontier moves fast.

Serving big models needs distributed inference: tensor parallelism splits individual layers across GPUs (needs fast interconnect like NVLink), pipeline parallelism splits layers across nodes, and expert parallelism shards mixture-of-experts models. Multi-node serving also involves quantization choices, autoscaling on GPU pools, and KV-cache-aware routing. The economics question in interviews: GPU utilization — idle GPUs are the biggest cost, hence continuous batching.

Scaling an AI system to high traffic: continuous batching on optimized runtimes (vLLM), multi-region replica fleets behind load balancers, semantic caching to absorb repeat queries (often 30-60% hit rate in support workloads), smaller distilled models for simple traffic tiers, and graceful degradation (queue, shorter context, fallback model). Capacity plan from tokens/sec per GPU, not request counts — and load-test with production-shaped traffic.

Responsible AI in practice: audit training data and outputs for bias (performance parity across demographic groups, not just averages); document models and data (model cards, datasheets); design for human oversight in consequential decisions (credit, hiring, healthcare — the model recommends, a person decides); red-team for misuse; and monitor post-deployment for disparate impact. Fairness definitions conflict mathematically (calibration vs equal error rates cannot both hold with unequal base rates), so choose deliberately with stakeholders.

AI safety and alignment: RLHF and constitutional approaches steer models toward helpful-and-harmless behavior; evaluations probe dangerous capabilities (cyber, bio) before release; guardrails and usage policies restrict harmful uses; research targets honesty (calibrated uncertainty), robustness (no brittle jailbreaks), and scalable oversight (humans supervising systems smarter than them). Interview framing: safety is engineering practice (threat modeling, evals, monitoring) plus governance (policies, audits) — not a one-time filter.

Streaming in chat UX: server-sent events (SSE) or WebSockets push tokens as generated, the client renders progressively with a cursor; perceived latency drops dramatically even when total time is unchanged. Engineering details: flush per token not per sentence, handle aborted generations (stop button cancels upstream to save cost), render markdown incrementally, and keep a non-streaming fallback for API clients that cannot consume streams.
